entries.english: The 13 Historical Giriama Circumcision Cycles (Marika, Taylor 1891 pp. 2, 21)
entries.translation: (1) Wula-mbere ('First-rains'), (2) Wula-kahi ('Middle-rains'), (3) Wula-nyuma ('Latter-rains'), (4) T'ungudza ('Tomatoes'), (5) P'uku ('Large wild rats'), (6) Nguluwe ('Pigs'), (7) Vitambi ('Coloured cloths'), (8) Vitsoka ('Hatchets'), (9) Abi-Kizi ('Kizi's-father'), (10) Atsai ('Wizards'), (11) Mafira ('Puff-adders'), (12) Mitseka ('Mats'), (13) Nyoga ('Feathers' — current cycle in 1891, with 'Kavuta' as its 1st sub-rika)
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', p. 2 under Age & p. 21 under Circumcision-cycles

entries.english: Giriama Elder Governance & Initiation Lodge Degrees (Habasi & K'ambi, Taylor 1891 pp. 37–38, 79)
entries.translation: Preliminaries: Uhoho → Umondo → Ubora | 1st Degree Habasi (Ahoho a Habasi-ni / Nyere under hierophant Muhagizi → Ahoho a Mihaso-ni) | 4 Dances to 2nd Degree K'ambi: (1) Gawe (with Mwandza M'kulu mystic drum under M'kuzi), (2) Sayo ra K'oma (under Mwenye Sayo), (3) M'ng'aro, (4) Kirao (with musichana bamboo drum; wearing luwoo armlet at Nyambura feast & sitting in M'oro parliament) | Senior Elders (Azhere): Waya (bandari club-house) & Fisi ('Hyena' inner circle under M'kuzi, then Mwa-Rima) → 3 Enye-ts'i ('Possessors of the Land')
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', pp. 37–38 under Freemasonry & p. 79 under Orders

entries.english: The 30-Day Giriama Month (3 Makumi), 4-Day Market/Farming Week & Seasons (Taylor 1891 pp. 56, 103, 134)
entries.translation: 3 Decades (Makumi): kumi ra kwandza, kumi ra kahi, kumi ra kuzimu (new moon hailed with 'Ko——ngo!') | 4-Day Week: (1) Jumwa, (2) Kuramuka, (3) Kurima-hiri, (4) Kuisa | 6-Day Future Sequence (p. 103): rero, machero, muhondo, gorya, mweriyao, mweriyao wa tuto | Seasons (p. 134): Mwaka (March/April Great Rains), Mwaka Musha (Ingathering), Mutsuwo (July/August Lesser Rains), Vuri (October Latter Rains, 1st month Kutsano)
entries.pronunciation: jum-wa, ku-ra-mu-ka, ku-ri-ma-hi-ri, ku-i-sa / mwa-ka, mu-tsu-wo, vu-ri
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', p. 56 under Moon, p. 103 under Time & p. 134 under Year

entries.english: The 12 Traditional Wanika (Mijikenda) Agricultural Months Across Masika, Furi & Kaskazi (Krapf 1882, p. 205 under masíka)
entries.translation: Masika & Furi (April–Nov, 8 farming months): (1) Muezi wa muanzo wa muaka (April — sowing mahindi), (2) Muezi wa viri (May), (3) Muezi wa tahu (June — maize ripens), (4) Muezi wa nne (July — first harvest; furi begins), (5) Muezi wa tzano (Aug — second sowing of maize), (6) Muezi wa handáhu (Sept), (7) Muezi wa fungáhu (Oct), (8) Muezi wa nane (Nov — second harvest) • Madjira ya kaskázi (Dec–March, 4 festival/dry months): (9) Muézi wa matzúla (Dec — tapping coconut palms), (10) Kurri bómu / kurri wa muanzo (Jan — great festival, no field work), (11) Kurri ya magáro (Feb — youth age-grade festival), (12) Muezi wa bózo / Muisho wa kaskazi (March — playing the záyo fiddle before clearing plantations)
entries.pronunciation: mweh-zee wah mwah-n-zoh wah mwah-kah ... koo-rree boh-moo ... mweh-zee wah boh-zoh
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf (1882) 'A Dictionary of the Suahili Language', p. 205 under masíka & Krapf & Rebmann (1887)

entries.english: Classical Giriama Adult & Aged Salutations (Taylor 1891 pp. 83–84)
entries.translation: Adult (any time): Voro! — Voro! Muzima? — M'zima. — Ndo vidzo! — Simanya na-we. — A! na-mi ni m'zīma | Aged Morning: Lam'kani! — Hmwishamwe. Mudzalamuka? — Hudzalamuka. — Na hulamuke! | Aged Midday: Tsanani! — Hmwishamwe! Mudzadherwa? — Hudzadherwa. — Na hudherwe! | Aged Evening: Dziloni! — Hmwishamwe! Kwatswa? — Kudzatswa! | Parting: Kala uworo! — Haya, enda matsiya!
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', pp. 83–84 under Salutation

entries.english: The 3 Geographical Divisions & 70 Districts (Malalo) of Giryama (Taylor 1891 pp. v–viii)
entries.translation: 1. Weruni (15 malalo: Papea, Mizaheni, Kadzitsoni, Manja, Kibwabwani, Ts'angalaweni ['muvirya' Gate to Kaya-Giryama], Kinagoni, Gotani, Kitswa-cha-Ndzovu, Bĭrini, Makululu, M'tsengo, Kirima cha Kitsomeni, Luvoli, Mwa-Ngongo & C.M.S. Kam'likeni) | 2. Central Giryama (31 malalo: Makonje-mare, Dungicha, Kaziya-m'oyo, Sosoni, Mitangoni, M'che K'endzi, Mihandeni, Mgamboni, M'uyuni, Mereni, Migujini, Bamba, Bi-Rya, Mutomo wa Bi-Rya, Silaloni, Mweza-m'oyo, Mitangani, Mutomo wa Mitangani, Maziya-Chenda ['Nine Pools'], Vigongeni, Mwaina, Peta-nguwo, Mweza, Nyari, Kakuluni, Ziya ra Mawe, Kita, Wacho, Malomani, Muhoni kwa Kadzina, Muhoni kwa Nyungu) | 3. Northern Giryama & Mt. Mangea (24 malalo: Kaziya-M'oyo, M'kauma-K'endzi [Kauma origin 'Hudzire hu-kauma'], M'tsangamale, Magogoni, Nyari, Rare kwa Mwavuwo, Dindiri kwa Ngonyo, Sinikumbe, Ts'angalaweni, Mangea [ancestral seat of Giryama & Taita], Mangea-wa-Nyasi, Kwa Mwana wa Gulicha, Soso-Demu, Mihuhuni, Fuladoyo [Galla 'fuldoya' looking-glass], Migodomani, Kalandzeni, Mwavueni, Mwanguďo, Soso-Dima, Mikalazani, Warawo, Mizijini)
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', Introduction pp. v–viii

entries.english: Giryama Phonology: Open vs. Close Minimal Pairs, Voiceless Nasals & N-Blending Explosives (Taylor 1891 pp. viii–xiv)
entries.translation: Minimal pairs (p. ix): tsama (be sweet) vs. ts a ma (migrate); laya (plant) vs. l a ya (forget); mwezi (cleansing) vs. mw e zi (moon); mweri (pure) vs. mw e ri (brass disc); fisi (hyena) vs. f i si (back of house); sīswi (not we) vs. s í swi (we); lukolo (filthy) vs. luk o lo (clan); ulongo (clay soil) vs. ul o ngo (lie); k a la (be) vs. kāla (stay/dwell) | Voiceless nasals (p. x): hmama, hnane, hvivi, hvoya, hmwinyi, hmwishamwe | Explosives (p. xii): p'ala vs. kapala, t 'iya vs. ka t iya, ts'ongo vs. katsongo, t'ahu vs. hahu, ch'ache vs. vichache, k'olo vs. lukolo | Falsetto ideophones (p. xiv): Mwaruhe tsé! (snow-white), mutune do! (bright red), mwiru pi! (jet-black), yunyemere myá-myá-myá! (dead silent)
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', Introduction pp. viii–xiv

entries.english: The 12 Giryama Noun Classes, 8 Derivative Verb Forms & Possessive of Alienation -ngwa (Taylor 1891 pp. xvii–xxv, 9–12, 65)
entries.translation: 12 Noun Classes: I mu-/a- (mut'u/at'u, subj. ni,u,yu/hu,mu,ma, neg. si,k'u,k'a/k'ahu,k'amu,k'ama), II mu-/mi- (muhi/mihi, u/i), III N/N (nyumba, i/zi), IV ki-/vi- (kit'u/vit'u, ki/vi), V -/ma- (tsoka/matsoka, ri/ga), VI Augmentative ri-(ridzi-)/mi- (ritsoka/mitsoka, ri/i, ku-kuga p. 41), VII lu-/ny- (lufu/nyufu, lu/zi), VIII Diminutive ka-(kadzi-)/u-(udzi-) (katsoka/utsoka, ka/u), IX u-/ma- (ut'u/maut'u, u/ga), X ha- (hat'u, near place), XI ku- (kufwa/kut'u, infinitive/distant place), XII mu- (mumu, interior) | 8 Verbal Derivatives: (1) Causative (-ya/-nya/-sa/-za/-sha/-zha), (2) Resultant (-ika/-eka), (3) Applied (-ira/-era), (4) Reciprocal (-na), (5) Reflexive (-dzi-), (6) Subtractive/Reversive (-ula/-ola), (7) Reduplicated, (8) Intensive enclitic -t'o (ku-hendá-t'o) | Alienation suffix -ngwa (pp. 65, 71): tsoka-ngwa (pl. ma-tsoka-ngwa, someone else's axe), vit'ungwa (other people's property)
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', pp. xvii–xxvii, 9–12, 41, 65, 71 & Table I–II

entries.english: The 10 Growth Stages of the Domestic Fowl (K'uku, Taylor 1891 p. 36) & Traditional Guilds (p. 133)
entries.translation: 10 Stages of Fowl: (1) kakuku katsanga → (2) kabuta → (3) kadzonya → (4) kahepe → (5) k'ereng'endze → (6) k'wahe → (7) mitsandzo → (8) p'ora (young cockerel) / mufaranga (pullet) → (9) majogolo (cock) / muhehera (laying hen) → (10) p'ungu (old cock) / kolo ra k'uku (full-grown hen) | Crafts (p. 133): urisa (herding), utsongi (carpentry), usanye (smithing), ukot'i/ususi (chain/mat-making), ugit'i (cooking/brewing), uasi (building), uhambi (travelling), uindza (hunting), uhegi (trapping), uk'urima (farming), ujema (palm-wine tapping), utsimbi wa mihaso (herb-gathering), uumbi (pottery/tobacco), upizi wa ts'andzi (collecting dues), uganga (medicine), upigi wa mburuga (divination), uenye-ts'i (governing)
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', p. 36 under Fowl & p. 133 under Work

entries.english: Giryama Proverbs in Rev. W. E. Taylor's 'African Aphorisms' (1891, §§ 601–633, pp. 136–143)
entries.translation: #601 Ambiri mako, asikiri k'amako (Tellers there are, listeners there are none) • #602 Bandzu, bandzu rámala gogo (Chip, chip finished the block) • #602a Chuwo k'akina mumwenga (Counsel is not of one only) • #603 Fisi rikirya m'kongo, m'zima funga nyumba (When the hyena eats the sick man, O well man, shut up your house) • #606 Kilagane kilagane! Simba k'arya mwana-we (A promise is a promise! The lioness eats not her own cub) • #611 Maneno madzo gausa ndzovu m'nda-ni (Fair speeches turn elephants out of the garden-patch) • #620 Mulungu wahumba, ela hundariwa ni-Ts'i (God created us, but we shall be consumed by Earth) • #621 Mwaka ni hmama, Vuri ni ami-somo (The March Rains are my mother, the Latter Rains my cousin's mother) • #623 Mwenda-mbere k'aheka madzi vundzu (The first to arrive draws no muddy water) • #630 T'embe na t'embe ni mukahe (Grain and grain makes a cake)
entries.pronunciation: ban-dzu ban-dzu ra-ma-la go-go / chu-wo k'a-ki-na mu-mwen-ga
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'African Aphorisms; or, Saws from Swahili-Land', Giryama Proverbs §§ 601–633, pp. 136–143

entries.english: The 22 Classical Giryama Riddles (Ndumo za Kigiryama, Taylor 1891 pp. 76–77, 138–140, #1–#22)
entries.translation: Challenge: Chondoni! — Response: Dekeha! (Forfeit if unguessed: P'a mudzi! — Haya enda Kisiwani!) • #1 Baba wákot'a kizimba dzulu ya m'uyu. — Ni p'ula (Father nailed a beehive on the baobab. — The nose) • #2 Bamba k'a lwayo. — Ni iwe (Mr. Flat has no footprint. — A rock) • #3 Choga m'zinga ts'ulu. — Ni sikiro (Fungus round the anthill. — The ear) • #4 Enda na kuno na-mi nenda na kuno, hukatunganane mugolokolo-ni. — Ni fiho za kipesa (Wall sticks) • #5 Fumo ra Mwa-Tela ridunga kosi-kosi. — Ni muts'i (Pestle) • #6 Fw-alume ahahu, akiuka mumwenga, k'afurya wari. — Ni mafigo (Three hearth-stones) • #7 Hawe nereka. — Ni uriri (Bedstead) • #8 K'akilumika. — Ni kikokora (Elbow) • #9 K'akioneka. — Ni k'ogo (Back of the head) • #10 K'akiuka-ts'i. — Ni kisima (Well) • #13 K'uku wa baba ugwiza miya-ni. — Ni ndimu (Lime-fruit) • #15 Kurima m'nda m'bomu ela ukadza vuna loya. — Ni nyere (Shaved hair) • #18 Magoma mairi lwanda-ni. — Ni mahombo (Breasts) • #20 Mbala na mwana-we madzakugonyeza k'unde-zo. — Ni sago na lwalwa (Upper and nether millstone) • #21 Mudhao mure k'aufunga k'uni. — Ni ngira (Path) • #22 Mwa-Mbita, kilolongo! — Ni viguzo zha kipesa (Wall posts)
entries.pronunciation: cho-ndo-ni / de-ke-ha / ba-ba wa-ko-t'a ki-zi-mba — ni p'u-la
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', pp. 76–77 under Riddle & Appendix pp. 138–140 (#1–#22)

entries.english: The 5 Classical Giryama Folktales & Origin Myths (Ngano za Kigiryama, Taylor 1891 Appendix pp. 129–138)
entries.translation: I. Katsungula na Simba (The Little Hare and the Lion — tricking Tortoise [Kobe] & Snouted Rat [Fugu] at the beehives [myato], and crying 'Alume-e-e! ts'i ii idzamera meno!'; closing charm: 'Ngano yangu igomera haha: Mwehu nyumba-ni muna ts'azi ya nyaa', pp. 129–132) • II. Fisi na Simba na Katsungula (The Hyena, the Lion, and the Little Hare — Hare refutes the Lion's claim that his bull bore a calf by running with calabashes saying his father gave birth: 'Mulume ni kuzhala-dze?', pp. 132–134) • III. K'uku na Katsungula (The Fowl and Harey — Fowl hides his head under his wing pretending his herd-boys [arisa] took it to pasture; Harey has his own head cut off and perishes, pp. 134–136) • IV.1 Kuononga kwa Muche (The Havoc Wrought by the Woman — curious wife spies behind a baobab [kolo ra m'uyu] on the headless animals cultivating the fields, who drop their hoes and turn into baboons [nyani] and monkeys [k'ima], pp. 136–137) • IV.2 Kuandika kwa Kufwa (The Origin of Death — Mulungu sends Lumbwi the Chameleon with 'Muzhalane ela matsafwa' [Multiply and die not], but Mugak'a the Lizard outruns him with 'Muzhalane ela mufwe!', pp. 137–138)
entries.pronunciation: nga-no za ki-gi-rya-ma / ka-tsu-ngu-la / lu-mbwi na mu-ga-k'a
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', Appendix pp. 129–138

entries.english: Sacred Friction Drum of the Kaya Elders & Ancestral Memorial Post
entries.translation: Mwandza M'kulu (sacred Kaya friction drum of the Gawe degree, p. 38) & kigango (pl. vigango, carved memorial post)
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891, p. 38) & Krapf & Rebmann (1887) 'A Nika-English Dictionary'

entries.english: Nyika (Rabai, Ribe & Digo) Proverbs in Rev. W. E. Taylor's 'African Aphorisms' (1891, §§ 634–664, pp. 144–159)
entries.translation: #634a Angwe—ndugu-ye ni ulongo ('They say' is own brother to a lie; kikulu ni kuona mwenye na matso) • #635 Cha muchia k'achenda / Digo: Ra munyonge k'arenda (The poor man's cultivation prospers not) • #637a Madzi gakimwagika, k'agadzoreka (When water is spilt, it cannot be gathered up) • #639 M'oro mudzo k'aulavya dzuwa (A good palaver does not let the sun rise high) • #640a Muhi ukigwa uegemera muya-we (When a tree falls it leans on its neighbour) • #644 Mwana-ts'i k'avundza-ts'i (The child of the land destroys not the land) • #647b Njira mbiri k'azituwika, záremeza fisi (Two roads cannot be followed at once, they were too much for the hyena) • #656 U nga nundu (You are like the bat — neither bird nor beast) • #660 Usena ukira udugu (Friendship surpasses relationship)
entries.pronunciation: cha mu-chi-a k'a-chen-da / nji-ra mbi-ri k'a-zi-tu-wi-ka / u-se-na u-ki-ra u-du-gu
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'African Aphorisms; or, Saws from Swahili-Land', Nyika Proverbs §§ 634–664, pp. 144–159 (with Rebmann 1887 citations)

entries.english: History of Kaya Mutzi Muíru on Mount Reale, Vokéra, Mutzi Múvia (Rabai M'pia) & the Two Mijikenda Brother-Tribe Confederacies (Krapf 1882, pp. 268–269)
entries.translation: Ancient Rabai capitals on Mount Reale: Mutzi Muíru (Mutzi mubomu wa Reale) & Mutzi Mudide (later called Mitzi ya Ntzoáni, led by fierce elders Gníro & Nchira); Malando & Kamfuda clans dispersed to Rombo in Chagga, Wadigo, and the Pokomo river, while one division sought refuge with their brother-tribe Chogni (Chogni cha Muadarúko), founded Kaya Vokéra for 9 generations, and later founded Mutzi Múvia (Rabbai M'pia) • Two Brother-Tribe Confederacies: (I) Muravai, Muchogni, Mukiriama, Mtahe; (II) Duruma, Rive, Kambe, Káuma • War-Council at Tziwe ra kizungu & Kizúmo / Salala Chant against Rabai Maboma: 'hukutáne, huenende, hukafunse mutzi hio wa Aravai' → 'Muravai! kuna ndugu! (Chorus: Ho-o!) Ndugúyo ni uha! Uhao ni nduguyo, Kuna ndúgu Muana 'Damu!' • Kóke ya motto / Tange (pp. 166–167, 359, 425): burning new forest clearings with Wawe song ('Wawe koke mana malíme') andRangáite dance (p. 314)
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf (1882) 'A Dictionary of the Suahili Language', pp. 166–167, 268–269 (under mutzi muíru), 314, 359, 425

entries.english: Dr. Krapf's (1850, p. vi) Wanika Ethnography, Mulungu Cosmology & Origin Traditions (Jagga, Ambakómo, Mángea)
entries.translation: Wanika Population & Polity (p. vi): ~50,000–60,000 souls living in woodland villages at 1,200–2,000 ft elevation, 15–20 miles inland between 3° and 5° S, governed by a republican council of elders (azee / kambi), believing in a Supreme Being called Mulungu ("heaven") and offering sacrifices at ancestral graves (koma) • Four Historical Migration Traditions (p. vi): (1) Rabbai (Rabai) claim their ancestors emigrated from Jagga (Kilimanjaro), where a related tribe still bears their name; (2) Wateita of Kadiáro, Ndara, and Bura call the Wanika "Ambakómo" because part of the Wanika formerly lived in the country of Pokómo (Tana River) before fleeing the Galla; (3) Wasegéju near Tanga likewise claim descent from Wapokómo expelled by the Galla; (4) Kiriama (Giriama) assert their forefathers lived at Mount Mángea near the Pokomóni
entries.pronunciation: wa-ni-ka / mu-lun-gu / ra-bba-i / a-mba-ko-mo / wa-se-ge-ju / ki-ri-a-ma / ma-nge-a
entries.context: Rev. Dr. J. L. Krapf (1850) 'Vocabulary of Six East-African Languages' (Tübingen), Preface p. vi
entries.culturalNote: Documents the earliest written record (October 14, 1850) of the Mijikenda/Pokomo/Segeju Tana-River and Mangea origin traditions alongside the Rabai-Chagga tradition.

categories.name: Kinika / Mijikenda Historical Lexicon & Ethnography (Krapf & Rebmann 1887)
categories.description: Kinship, teknonymy (Abe-/Ame-), kaya architecture (mumfiria, m'oro, rungu), the 4 kihendo age-grade orders, 13 solar time divisions (dzua), 7 coconut growth stages, 9 palm-wine calabash sizes (kibaria), crop-specific harvesting verbs, judicial ordeals (kiravo), and ritual traditions from Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann's A Nika-English Dictionary (1887).

entries.english: Father of — / Mother of — (teknonymic titles taken from the firstborn child, e.g., Abe-Gunja, Abe-Chindua Muambawa, Abe-Mkusi Dzama, Amegnania; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, pp. 1, 6)
entries.translation: Father of — / Mother of — (teknonymic titles taken from the firstborn child, e.g., Abe-Gunja, Abe-Chindua Muambawa, Abe-Mkusi Dzama, Amegnania; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, pp. 1, 6)
entries.context: Upon the birth of a firstborn child (muahuladzansu / musunduladzansu / mimba mbere), parents drop their youth names and are addressed as Abe-[Child] and Ame-[Child], while Baba and Mayo are used for direct address.
entries.culturalNote: Upon the birth of a firstborn child (muahuladzansu / musunduladzansu / mimba mbere), parents drop their youth names and are addressed as Abe-[Child] and Ame-[Child], while Baba and Mayo are used for direct address.

entries.english: paternal aunt (father's sister; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, pp. 57, 333)
